passage:
Dear Ganga,

I've been thinking about what you did last month when Baba was in hospital and I couldn't keep up with my classes. You didn't say much, just "I'm here." Then you turned up with your notes every evening, sat with me in the corridor and stayed until visiting hours ended. When I forgot to eat you left a tiffin at my door. I don't think I said thank you properly.

I also want to say something honest. When you told me you'd lied to your manager about being unwell, I kept quiet, and I regret it. I care about you too much to pretend that was okay.

Your friend,
Tushar

qa.q: What did Ganga leave at Tushar's door?
qa.a: Ganga left a tiffin at Tushar's door.

qa.q: What does Tushar feel about having kept quiet about the lie?
qa.a: Tushar regrets staying silent, and wants to be honest because of caring about Ganga. Loyalty here means being truthful, not hiding a problem.

qa.q: What could Ganga do with Tushar's honest note?
qa.a: Read it as care, talk with Tushar about the situation at work, and think about what to say to the manager.

qa.q: How might Ganga feel receiving both thanks and honesty?
qa.a: Ganga may feel warm about the thanks and perhaps uneasy about the honesty, but the letter shows the friendship can handle both.

grounding: A young adult shows care through time, help and follow-through, and shows loyalty that allows honesty.

passage: You asked me on the podcast what loyalty looks like, so let me tell you about Elizabeth. Salma here. When my father lost his job, she didn't send flowers or big words. She texted, "Can I come over on Thursday with dinner?" She came, washed the dishes, listened for two hours and then asked the next week how the interviews went. That follow-through meant more than any speech. But loyalty also means honesty. When I told her I'd been hiding a debt from my family, she didn't say "I'll keep your secret." She said, "I'll help you tell them, and I'll stand next to you." That was harder, and it was real.

qa.q: On which day did Elizabeth come over with dinner?
qa.a: Elizabeth came over on Thursday with dinner.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth's follow-up show about her care?
qa.a: It showed she cared beyond the first visit, since she asked the next week how the interviews went. Salma feels the follow-through mattered more than words.

qa.q: What could Salma do next about the hidden debt?
qa.a: Tell her family with Elizabeth beside her, and ask for a trusted adult's help with the problem.

qa.q: How might Salma's family have felt on learning about the debt?
qa.a: They might be surprised or worried at first, but hearing it from Salma with a friend's support is likely better than finding out by accident.

grounding: A young adult shows care through follow-through, and loyalty that allows honesty rather than silence about harm.

passage: I'm Sarita, and I live across the corridor from Anand in the colony. I don't know him well, but I watched what he did last winter when his friend Mahesh had knee surgery. Anand didn't post anything online or make speeches. He just came. Every evening after work he climbed the three floors with a tiffin. On Sundays he took Mahesh's scooter to be serviced and paid his electricity bill at the counter. When Mahesh's physiotherapy started, Anand drove him on Tuesdays and Fridays, and waited outside for an hour each time, reading. Once I heard them arguing: Mahesh wanted to skip the exercises, and Anand said, quite firmly, "No. I'm not helping you get worse." I don't know what Anand felt; he always looked tired but cheerful. By spring, Mahesh was walking to the gate to meet him. I still think about it when people talk about friendship.

qa.q: On which days did Anand drive Mahesh to physiotherapy?
qa.a: Tuesdays and Fridays.

qa.q: What might Anand have been feeling through the winter?
qa.a: Sarita can't be sure, but Anand looked tired yet cheerful, suggesting he felt worn out but content and committed to helping his friend.

qa.q: What does Anand's care teach about being a good friend?
qa.a: Care shows in time, practical help and follow-through, and loyalty includes honesty, like pushing Mahesh to do his exercises.

qa.q: How might Mahesh have felt about Anand's firm "No"?
qa.a: He may have felt annoyed in the moment, but by spring he was walking to the gate to meet Anand, suggesting he felt grateful.

grounding: Shows through an observer a young adult expressing care through time, help and follow-through, with loyalty that allows honesty.

passage:
Monday. Samir's father died suddenly, and Kavitha heard from a classmate. She didn't know what to say, so she didn't post anything. She went to his house, left a steel box of lemon rice with his aunt, and said, "Tell him Kavitha came. No need to reply."
Thursday. She messaged Samir: "I've got your lecture notes for this week. Will drop them at the gate at six." She did, and left without ringing the bell.
Three weeks later. Samir came back to college. At lunch, he admitted he'd been skipping meals and feeling "like a ghost". Kavitha listened. Then she said, honestly, "I'm worried about the meals. Can I tell your cousin, or will you?" Samir hesitated. "I'll tell her. Tonight." "Okay. I'll ask you tomorrow if you did." The next day she asked. He had. She passed him half her sandwich anyway.

qa.q: What did Kavitha leave with Samir's aunt?
qa.a: A steel box of lemon rice.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling when he came back to college?
qa.a: He felt numb and lost, "like a ghost", and was so low he was skipping meals.

qa.q: What did Kavitha do that showed real care?
qa.a: She gave time and practical help, followed through, and was honest about her worry, asking Samir to tell his cousin and checking the next day.

qa.q: What would change if Kavitha had stayed silent about the skipped meals to be loyal?
qa.a: Samir's cousin might never have known, and his skipping meals could have gone on without support.

grounding: Shows a young adult caring through presence, help and follow-through, and a loyalty that does not stay silent about harm.

passage: Aparna, you say your friend asked you to keep a secret. Let me tell you about Deepak, my closest friend in the engineering hostel, when I was twenty. Your Anand chacha loved that boy like a brother. We ate together, studied together, and I'd have done anything for him. Then one night he told me that a senior was making the first-years in his wing do push-ups at 2 a.m. and hitting the ones who refused. "Don't tell anyone, the seniors will make my life hell." I promised. For a week I couldn't sleep. I was torn. Being loyal to Deepak felt like being silent about boys getting hurt. So I went to Deepak first and said, "I'm going to tell the warden. I'll stand next to you the whole time." He was angry for two days. The warden acted that week. Deepak's still my friend, beta. Loyalty that asks you to hide harm is not loyalty.

qa.q: What was the senior making the first-years do at 2 a.m.?
qa.a: Push-ups, and hitting the ones who refused.

qa.q: How did young Anand feel during the week after he promised to keep the secret?
qa.a: He was torn and anxious, unable to sleep, because loyalty to Deepak clashed with staying silent about harm.

qa.q: What choice in the story stopped the ragging?
qa.a: Anand told Deepak he would go to the warden and stand by him, and the warden acted that week.

qa.q: How did Deepak react when Anand said he'd tell the warden?
qa.a: Deepak was angry for two days, probably scared of the seniors, but stayed Anand's friend.

grounding: Shows a young adult expressing loyalty that allows honesty and does not require silence about harm.

passage: The rain hadn't stopped for three days, and Chaitanya's scraped arm was still bandaged when Imran knocked with a steel tiffin of dal-chawal and the week's lecture notes. He had come every evening since the skid, missing his own cricket practice. Tonight Chaitanya pushed the notes aside. "Just don't tell anyone how it happened. Especially not my parents." Imran sat on the edge of the bed. He knew how it happened: two beers at Nikhil's party, then the bike on a wet road. "I'll bring food as long as your arm needs it. I'll copy every note," he said. "But I'm not keeping quiet if you ride after drinking again. That's not loyalty. That's watching you get hurt." Chaitanya stared at the rain. "You'd really tell?" "I'd tell. And I'm keeping your keys till the exams are over." He held out his hand. After a long moment, Chaitanya dropped the keys into it.

qa.q: What did Imran bring when he knocked?
qa.a: A steel tiffin of dal-chawal and the week's lecture notes.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when Chaitanya asked for silence?
qa.a: Imran felt torn: loyal and caring, but worried that staying quiet would mean watching Chaitanya get hurt again.

qa.q: How did Imran combine loyalty with honesty?
qa.a: He kept caring in practical ways, with food, notes and time, while refusing to stay silent about riding after drinking and taking the keys until the exams.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya have felt handing over the keys?
qa.a: Probably ashamed and a little cornered, but also cared for, since Imran's daily help showed the demand came from love.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult showing care through time, help and follow-through, and a loyalty that allows honesty instead of silence about harm.
